scenario: Today's retrieval track asks whether the retrieval object actually matches the task a user is trying to finish, and whether the result can be inspected. One paper turns query rewriting into a searchable strategy, so prompts and decoding parameters evolve with retrieval feedback. Another breaks medical dense vectors into interpretable sparse features that can explain why a document was returned. Public-interest search over governance documents insists on binding answers to the exact text and edition, and a digital-library study embeds both the figures and the text of scanned pages. Other work writes reading progress as a spoiler boundary, first assigns a finance agent's failures to the layer that should be fixed, and measures how much local paper search depends on the model and on how specific the query is. Medication prediction from health records retrieves a population prior instead of similar patients, and visual question answering first judges whether a reference is clear before deciding how to answer.

papers.title: RAG-FGO: Dynamic Optimization of Query-Rewriting Agents for Generative RAG
papers.authors: Qigan Sun, Xudong Wang, Chaoning Zhang, Chenghao Li, Jiaquan Zhang, Jiehui Xie, Sungyoung Lee, Jie Zou, Ning Xie, Peng Wang, Yang Yang, Heng Tao Shen
papers.abstract: In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), query rewriting serves as a core interface that aligns user intent with external knowledge bases, and its effectiveness directly determines overall system performance. However, generative retrieval faces three critical challenges in real-world deployment: noisy retrieval feedback, the difficulty of jointly optimizing discrete prompt templates and continuous decoding-control parameters, and the limited generalization of static rewriting strategies under semantically complex scenarios. To address these issues, we propose RAG-FGO, a dynamic optimization framework for generative retrieval strategies. RAG-FGO formulates query rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box optimization problem in a mixed discrete-continuous space, and represents prompt templates and decoding parameters as adaptively optimizable query-rewriting agents. The framework performs global search to enable semantic jumps and structural reorganization that escape local optima, whi
papers.summary: In retrieval-augmented generation, rewriting the user question is supposed to make retrieval more accurate, but retrieval feedback is often noisy, prompt text and decoding parameters such as temperature must be tuned together, and a fixed strategy breaks down on semantically complex questions. The authors treat rewriting as a non-differentiable black-box problem: prompt templates and decoding parameters become rewriting agents that can be updated iteratively, with a global search to escape local optima, local refinements, and a memory pool that keeps strong strategies to resist noise. With GPT-4o-mini as the generator, mean answer-level F1 on six question-answering benchmarks rises from 68.9 for the strongest retrieval baseline to 77.1. ==A rewriting strategy should be searched with retrieval feedback, not frozen as one prompt in advance==. For teams serving retrieval-augmented question answering, prompts and generation parameters can be maintained as an evolving rewriting module, rather than by hand-trying a few templates.

papers.title: Explanations that Transfer: Interpreting Medical Retrieval with Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.abstract: Medical AI systems that answer users' queries rely on retrieving medical knowledge from large document collections. In this context, finetuning general models on medical datasets can improve retrieval relevance. Yet the dense embeddings underlying modern retrieval systems remain largely opaque, making it difficult to understand the mechanics behind their results. Moreover, adapting to a specific medical dataset risks losing transferability to new clinical corpora. In this work, we tackle these issues by applying Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to medical information retrieval, transforming dense text embeddings into semantically interpretable representations. To do so, our model combines a reconstruction objective with an InfoNCE contrastive loss that directly preserves query-document relevance. We evaluate three embedding models across six medical retrieval datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the origina
papers.summary: Medical question answering first has to retrieve relevant passages from large document collections, but the dense vectors in common use are almost impossible to explain, and fine-tuning on one corpus often loses performance on a new clinical collection. The authors use sparse autoencoders to turn dense text vectors into interpretable features, training both to reconstruct the original vectors and, with a contrastive loss, to keep query-document relevance. On the CURE medical training set, NDCG@10 with BGE embeddings rises from 53.06 to 61.87. With sparse features, the drop on unseen medical retrieval sets is also smaller, and the meaning of a feature can be read from the queries and documents that activate it most, which helps explain why a document was retrieved. ==Medical retrieval should not only be more accurate; it should also be able to say why this document was returned==. For teams serving medical retrieval, interpretable sparse features help inspect results and reduce overfitting to a new corpus.

papers.title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
papers.authors: Snehalkumar `Neil', Dhruv Dixit, Bryen Alvarez, Pratik Patekar, Anika Sharma, Akshara Kolipaka, Paritosh Pandey S. Gaikwad
papers.abstract: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents.
papers.summary: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence, often defining what counts as an automated decision or a harm before the people affected have a chance to question them. The authors build a public-interest system that turns thousands of governance documents, from cities to national governments, into passages that keep their page and edition, and uses bounded agentic search to verify each cited statement. A resident can look up the city's rules on AI in hiring, or upload a national strategy, read it as an affected person would, and draft a revision. On new questions that require finding the relevant documents, macro-average recall reaches 83.0%, compared with 73.7% without iterative search. In a user study, most proposed changes asked how a provision would actually apply. ==Retrieval has to be bound to the exact text and edition of a public document before people can use it to discuss and revise the rules==. For public-policy retrieval, finding the right documents and giving checkable citations matters more than a fluent answer alone.

papers.title: Towards High-Performance Multimodal Discovery: Evaluating Retrieval Efficacy and Operational Scalability in Digital Libraries
papers.authors: Krishna Priya, Sai Navya Jyesta, Sachith Withana, Neelesh Karthikeyan, Beth Plale
papers.abstract: Large-scale digital repositories with million plus digitized volumes serve as vital engines for scientific and scholarly discovery. However, as collections grow, finding specific research or educational material remains a significant challenge. This difficulty is compounded by the multimodal nature of texts, that is, texts which combine dense narrative content with essential illustrative charts, annotated diagrams, and complex layouts. Historically, discovery has been supported by full-text search indexes implemented as inverted indexes (e.g., Lucene or Solr). While these systems scale well for textual strings, they are fundamentally "blind" to the semantic nuance of visual information. We explore the benefit of discovery through texts that have been converted to numerical vectors. By representing page images as numerical vectors rather than OCR-extracted text, and doing so for both text and images on a page, we capture both textual and visual semantics while mitigating reverse enginee
papers.summary: In large digital libraries, many holdings are scanned pages that mix text and figures. A full-text inverted index can barely see diagrams, tables, and layout, so text from optical character recognition alone misses key information. The authors embed each page image as a vector that carries both textual and visual semantics, retrieve with a vector database, and compare similarity functions. On the full benchmark, cosine similarity reaches a mean reciprocal rank of 0.801, clearly better than 0.418 for Euclidean distance, and it is especially suited to questions about diagrams or tables and to visually dense pages with little text. Retrieval precision itself is not high, so better reranking is still needed. When the corpus grows from one hundred pages to a little more than four thousand, latency rises only about twenty times, and throughput can exceed 3,500 queries per second. ==For mixed image-and-text collections, a text index is not enough; vector retrieval must also capture visual semantics==. For scholarly discovery systems, the point is not only a stronger vision model, but an index that can run at library scale.

papers.title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
papers.authors: Mohammed Efaz, Udo Bub, Itilekha Podder
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed pr
papers.summary: When a language model sits beside a reader, sending the whole book in at once makes it easy to reveal later plot points, and the text often has to be uploaded to the cloud. The authors build an offline reading assistant in which retrieval and generation are confined to the reader's current place in the text, and combine vector similarity, keyword matching, and summary embeddings so the answer stays with the current progress. On comprehension questions and spoiler checks from three English novels, mid-sized local models can reach comprehension quality close to larger counterparts. The strongest of them reach a BERT F1 of about 0.74 to 0.75, at about 30 seconds per item. A progress boundary is used to block unread content without giving up retrieval quality on what has already been read. ==A reading companion should move forward with the reader, not finish the book first and then answer==. For teams that want local reading support, writing progress as a boundary that both retrieval and generation must respect can protect privacy without spoiling the story.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Finance Agent? Drift, Diagnosis and Auditable Intervention on One Shipped Financial Research Agent
papers.authors: Cosimo Galeone, Anna Ettorre, Ginevra Mariani, Minsu Park, Giuseppe Ettorre, Daniele Ligorio
papers.abstract: Can you trust a finance agent you did not build? We take the reference agent shipped with the Vals Finance Agent Benchmark v2, leave it untuned, and ask four questions a leaderboard score does not answer. Is the score stable? Seven identical runs on 18 questions pass between 105 and 123 of 149 rubric criteria, and the bill varies by up to 17%. When the agent fails, who owns the fix? We classify 20 failed trajectories, from three runs of nine held-out questions, by the layer whose owner would remedy them, under a taxonomy frozen in advance: 13 belong to the agent's instructions, 3 to its tools, 4 to the model, none to its data. Can that diagnosis be trusted? Four blind readers from three model families, given only the traces, name the same fault as our LLM analyzer in 94% of cases, the rate at which they agree with one another (93%). Can a change be trusted? An optimization loop reads the traces, makes one targeted change per round and keeps it only if it clears a fixed threshold. Under
papers.summary: A single leaderboard score for a finance agent you did not build rarely says whether the system is stable, who should fix a failure, or whether a change can be trusted. The authors take an untuned reference agent and repeatedly run the same questions; the number of rubric criteria passed moves from 105 to 123, and the bill also varies clearly. Under a taxonomy frozen in advance, most failures belong to the agent's instructions, then to its tools and the model, and none to its data. An optimization loop that reads traces, changes one thing per round, and keeps it only past a fixed threshold cuts cost on the held-out questions to 0.34 times the baseline, with accuracy still within noise. A gain under an accuracy objective does not pass a test written before the run was opened. ==An agent's score must first survive repeated runs, before one asks what to change and whether the change is real==. This is a case study of one agent and a small test set, but it shows auditors how to measure noise and assign the responsible layer first.

papers.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
papers.authors: Frederic Andriantseheno Rakoto, Yannis Bendi-Ouis, Xavier Hinaut
papers.abstract: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally faster than the Mac Studio, but its unified memory allows larger models that could not be loaded in the tested GPU configuration.
papers.summary: If scientific literature search can run with a locally deployed language-model assistant, teams can send less data and infrastructure to a hosted provider. It is still unclear, though, whether open-weight models can actually retrieve papers under practical compute limits. The authors compare inference latency on a Mac Studio and on a two-GPU server, then have eight models search for 70 papers in seven repositories, with queries written at three levels of expertise. Retrieval success depends strongly on which model is chosen and how specific the query is: only 6.2% of basic phrasings succeed, while 48.2% of expert phrasings do. The server is usually faster, but the Mac's unified memory can load larger models that did not fit in the GPU configuration tested here. ==For local paper search, the model and how specific the query is often decide success more than a slightly faster platform==. For research groups that want their own literature assistant, testing models against their own query habits is more reliable than looking only at parameter counts or official demos.

papers.title: Lens: Training-Free Semantic Search for Cross-Tile Object and Scene Retrieval in Satellite Imagery
papers.authors: Ata Akbari Asanjan, Anit Upadhyaya, Jeremy Kravitz, Subash Yeggina
papers.abstract: We developed Lens, a training-free system for semantic object and scene search across large satellite mosaics that requires no detector trained for the class of interest. Lens represents each tile with a frozen, self-supervised vision transformer (DINOv3), removes the positional bias in its dense features by projecting them onto the subspace orthogonal to a positional basis estimated once from a constant image, and centers the debiased features on the mean feature computed across the whole area before comparison. Lens forms a query by averaging the centered features of a small neighborhood of patches around a chosen point, or of an entire tile for scene-level search, and matches it against the index by cosine similarity. It stores the centered patch features in a byte-quantized similarity index that supports real-time range search over a mosaic of thousands of patches, and a coarser whole-tile embedding index for scene-level retrieval. A guided upsampling network (AnyUp) runs once per
papers.summary: Semantic search for an object or scene in a large satellite mosaic usually starts by training a detector for that class, and a new class means doing the work again. The authors build a system that needs no further training for a new class: a frozen self-supervised vision model represents each tile, positional bias is removed, features are centered on the area mean, and matching uses cosine similarity. A query can be a small neighborhood around a click, or a whole tile for scene search, and finer boundaries are computed once and then cached. On a test set of a little more than five thousand tiles, mean pixel-level F1 is 0.39, with a large spread across classes. A click returns a rendered overlay in about 6 to 10 milliseconds. ==Even without a detector trained for this class, a clickable semantic index can first surface the candidates==. For interactive search over large remote-sensing mosaics, this replaces training a detector first with building a reusable feature index and searching from a click.

papers.title: Tabular Population Priors as Structured Retrieval for EHR Medication Set Prediction
papers.authors: Animesh Agarwal, Meysam Ghaffari, Nina Fatehi, Carlos Morato
papers.abstract: Medication prediction from electronic health records is a fixed vocabulary structured prediction problem, yet recent clinical RAG systems often treat it like open ended case based reasoning: retrieve similar patient admissions and ask an LLM to infer a medication set. This retrieval object is indirect the model receives retrieved patient records while the target is a discrete set of medication class labels. We propose a more task aligned retrieval object: a tabular population prior ranked medication class candidates from a sparse condition medication co occurrence table estimated from training admissions. Using PACERAG as a fixed downstream pipeline and replacing only its patient retriever, this drop in swap improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 on 1,004 heldout MIMIC IV admissions, with no additional LLM calls and no inference time patient index. A non LLM top k baseline reaches F1=0.248, confirming the prior is predictive before LLM integra
papers.summary: Predicting a medication set from electronic health records is a structured problem over a fixed vocabulary of drug classes, yet many clinical retrieval-augmented systems first fetch similar patients and then ask a language model to infer the medications. What is retrieved is a patient record, while the target is a discrete set of drug labels, so the two are not aligned. The authors instead use a tabular population prior estimated from condition-medication co-occurrence in the training data, listing candidate drug classes by co-occurrence strength, and replace only the patient retriever in an otherwise unchanged pipeline. On a little more than a thousand held-out admissions, F1 rises from 0.303 to 0.338, with no extra language-model calls and no patient index at inference time. The prior is already predictive before a language model is involved. ==For set prediction over a fixed vocabulary, the retrieval object should be candidates from that vocabulary, not a detour through similar patients==. For clinical medication prediction, population statistics are easier to audit and often a better fit to the task.

papers.title: AmbiSteer: Selectively Eliciting Ambiguity-Aware Responses in Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Monica Riedler, Samuele Antonelli, Barbara Plank, Raffaella Bernardi
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) often exhibit overconfidence, providing firm answers even when visual evidence is insufficient. A prominent case is referential ambiguity in Visual Question Answering (VQA), where multiple entities in an image are plausible referents of a question. Addressing such cases requires recognizing when ambiguity is present: ambiguous questions can be handled by asking for clarification or enumerating plausible referents, while unambiguous questions should receive a direct answer. Current VLMs struggle with this distinction, often defaulting to a single interpretation. To investigate whether activation steering can serve as an inference-time mechanism to elicit such behaviors, we introduce AmbiSteer, a lightweight framework to selectively elicit ambiguity-aware behavior. Across three VLMs, we find that steering alone has limited and model-dependent effects, while prompting is generally more effective. Combining prompting and steering substantially increases clarif
papers.summary: Vision-language models are often overconfident, giving a firm answer even when the visual evidence is not enough. A typical case is referential ambiguity in visual question answering: several objects in the image could be what the question refers to. The model should then ask a clarifying question or list the plausible referents, and should answer directly only when the reference is clear. Current models struggle with this distinction and often default to a single reading. The authors use activation steering at inference time to elicit awareness of ambiguity, and find that steering alone has limited, model-dependent effects, while prompting is usually more effective. Combining the two increases clarification and enumeration, but also triggers them on unambiguous cases. They therefore use a linear classifier to judge whether the input is ambiguous and to choose the steering direction, raising the share of inputs handled appropriately from 59.0% to 77.0% on average across models. ==A model should first decide whether the question is clear, and only then choose to answer, to ask, or to list the possibilities==. For multimodal question answering, this is a way to reduce overconfidence at inference time without retraining.
